specPoints.text: know that nuclear reactions, including fission, fusion and radioactive decay, can be a source of energy

primer.text: The nucleus is an energy vault: fusing small nuclei together, splitting large ones apart, or letting an unstable nucleus decay all open that vault and pour out energy. Stars run on fusion, power stations on fission, and every radioactive source leaks a little of the same store as it decays.

lessons.title: Sources of nuclear energy and fusion
lessons.opening: A nucleus packs away an enormous store of energy, and three kinds of reaction can release it: fusion, fission and radioactive decay. Fusion is the joining of two small nuclei into one larger nucleus — the reaction that lights the stars, where deuterium and tritium can merge into helium.
keyPoints: A nucleus holds a huge amount of energy that nuclear reactions can set free.
Fusion, fission and radioactive decay are the three sources of nuclear energy.
In fusion, two small nuclei join together and build one larger nucleus.
Deuterium and tritium, both isotopes of hydrogen, can fuse into a helium nucleus.
Fusion runs naturally in stars, but not in everyday conditions on Earth.

low.restatement: Fusion: two little nuclei become one bigger nucleus and give out energy.
low.analogy: Two small snowballs rolled into one bigger snowball — joining releases the squash.
low.examPointer: Learn the trio of nuclear energy sources — fusion, fission, decay — as one list.

medium.restatement: Fusion converts a sliver of mass into energy when light nuclei merge; deuterium and tritium are the classic hydrogen pair that produce helium.
medium.analogy: A crowded train carriage: squeezing two small groups into one seat-row releases shoving energy — the closer the packing, the bigger the release.
medium.examPointer: Quote the coal equivalence only as 'about ten million kilograms per kilogram of hydrogen' — it is an order-of-magnitude fact, not a precise conversion.

options.text: two small nuclei join to build a larger nucleus
options.explanation: Fusion is the merging of light nuclei.

options.text: one big nucleus dividing into two smaller ones
options.explanation: That is fission, the opposite process.

options.text: a nucleus releases a gamma ray only
options.explanation: Gamma decay changes no nucleus at all.

options.text: a neutron turns into a proton
options.explanation: That is beta decay inside a nucleus.

check.stem: Deuterium and tritium nuclei fuse together. What do they form?

options.explanation: Two hydrogen isotopes merge into helium, releasing energy.
Fission fuels are heavy nuclei; fusion builds light ones up.
The nuclei join; they do not stay apart.
Those are fission daughters of uranium.

check.stem: Where does nuclear fusion happen naturally?

options.explanation: Star cores are hot and dense enough for fusion to run by itself.
Reactors currently use fission; fusion reactors are still in development.
Atmospheric conditions are far too cool for fusion.
Ores decay, they do not fuse.

check.stem: The three sources of nuclear energy are…

options.explanation: All three open the energy stored in nuclei.
Burning and evaporation are chemical, not nuclear.
Combustion is chemical energy, not nuclear.
Photosynthesis stores light energy, not nuclear energy.

check.stem: Fusing 1 kg of hydrogen releases roughly the energy of burning…

options.explanation: The corpus equivalence for hydrogen fusion is about 10,000,000 kg of coal.
That underplays the yield by a factor of a thousand.
Fusion outshines coal by many orders of magnitude.
The stated factor is ten million, not one million.

check.stem: Name the three sources of nuclear energy.
check.modelAnswer: Nuclear fusion, nuclear fission and radioactive decay.

check.stem: State what forms when deuterium and tritium fuse.
check.modelAnswer: A helium nucleus forms, with a large release of energy.

check.stem: Explain why stars can power themselves by fusion but Earth cannot rely on natural fusion.
check.modelAnswer: Star cores reach temperatures and pressures far beyond anything found naturally on Earth, so hydrogen nuclei there collide hard enough to merge, while everyday Earth conditions stay far too cool and roomy for fusion to run by itself.

check.stem: A fusion trial consumes 2 kg of hydrogen. Using the coal equivalence, how many kilograms of coal would release the same energy?
check.modelAnswer: 1 kg of hydrogen fused matches about 10,000,000 kg of coal, so 2 kg matches 2 × 10,000,000 = 20,000,000 kg of coal.

lessons.title: Fission basics
lessons.opening: Fission is the mirror image of fusion: one heavy nucleus divides into a pair of smaller ones. The splitting nucleus is called the parent and the pieces are the daughters, and this is the reaction that today's nuclear power stations use to make electricity.
keyPoints: Nuclear fission: a heavy parent nucleus divides into two smaller daughter nuclei.
The splitting nucleus is the parent; the fragments are the daughter nuclei.
Fission is the process nuclear power stations use to generate electricity.
Like fusion, fission releases energy stored in the nucleus.

low.restatement: Fission: one big nucleus breaks into two smaller pieces and releases energy.
low.analogy: A packed suitcase bursting open: the single case (parent) splits into two smaller bags (daughters) that fly apart.
low.examPointer: Keep parent and daughter straight: parent splits, daughters are produced.

medium.restatement: Fission divides a large parent nucleus into two daughter nuclei, releasing nuclear energy that power stations convert into electricity.
medium.analogy: Splitting a log: one heavy piece becomes two lighter pieces, and the stored tension in the wood is released as the halves spring apart.
medium.examPointer: Power-station questions usually want the words fission, parent and daughter used precisely — name them, don't paraphrase.

check.stem: Nuclear fission is best described as…

options.text: one large nucleus splitting into two smaller nuclei
options.explanation: Fission divides a heavy parent into two daughters.

options.text: two small nuclei joining into one larger nucleus
options.explanation: That is fusion.

options.text: an atom losing an orbital electron
options.explanation: Electron loss is ionisation, not nuclear fission.

options.text: a nucleus releasing only gamma rays
options.explanation: Gamma emission leaves the nucleus unsplit.

check.stem: The fragments produced when a parent nucleus splits are called…

options.explanation: The split products carry the daughter name.
The parent is the nucleus that split, not the fragments.
The established term is daughters.
Beta particles are emitted electrons, not fragments.

check.stem: Which machines generate electricity from fission today?

options.explanation: Controlled fission is the working reactor technology.
Fusion reactors are in development, not yet commercial.
Coal burns chemically; no nuclei split.
Solar panels convert light, not nuclear energy.

check.stem: In fission, the large original nucleus is named the…

options.explanation: Parent is the established name for the splitting nucleus.
Daughters are the two fragments produced.
No such term exists in the topic.
The topic's word is parent.

check.stem: Which statement about fission energy is correct?

options.text: energy stored in the nucleus is released when it splits
options.explanation: The split frees nuclear energy, often as kinetic energy of the products.
Energy is released from a store, never conjured.

options.text: fission absorbs more energy than it gives back
options.explanation: Fission is a net energy release.
Fission also generates electricity in power stations.

check.modelAnswer: Nuclear fission is the splitting of one large nucleus into two smaller nuclei, with the release of energy.

check.stem: State where fission is used to generate electricity.
check.modelAnswer: Nuclear power stations use controlled fission to generate electricity.

check.stem: Explain why fusion and fission both count as sources of nuclear energy.
check.modelAnswer: Both reactions release the energy stored inside nuclei: fusion frees it when small nuclei merge, fission frees it when a large nucleus is split, so either route taps the same nuclear store.

check.stem: An engineer describes 'one heavy nucleus dividing into two lighter nuclei, with energy out'. Name the process and the fragment nuclei.
check.modelAnswer: The process is nuclear fission, and the two lighter product nuclei are the daughter nuclei of the parent.

glossary.definition: Joining of two small nuclei into one larger nucleus, releasing energy.
Splitting of one large nucleus into two smaller daughter nuclei, releasing energy.
A hydrogen isotope whose nucleus carries one proton and one neutron; a fusion fuel.
A heavier hydrogen isotope that can fuse with deuterium to make helium.
